title: Snakes and Ladders
directAnswer: This is a shortest-path problem on an unweighted graph, so the answer is BFS. Flatten the n×n board into squares 1…n² using boustrophedon (snake) numbering, where each square has up to 6 outgoing edges (a dice roll of 1–6) and snakes/ladders are forced jumps to another square. BFS from square 1 layer by layer; the first time you dequeue n² the layer count is the minimum number of moves. If you exhaust the queue without reaching n², return −1. O(n²) time and space.

remember.pattern: Shortest path on an unweighted implicit graph → BFS
rules: Each move = a dice roll, so every edge has **weight 1** → BFS gives the shortest path (not DFS, not Dijkstra).
Flatten 2D → 1D with **boustrophedon** numbering: rows alternate left-to-right and right-to-left, starting bottom-left.
From square `x` you can go to `x+1 … x+6`; a snake/ladder at the landing square is a **forced** jump (apply once, don't chain).
Mark a square **visited when you enqueue** it, keyed by its *final* destination, not the intermediate roll square.
Process the queue **one layer at a time** and increment `moves` per layer; the layer index is the distance.
whenToUse: Fewest steps / minimum moves on an unweighted board or grid
Shortest transformation where each step has equal cost
Implicit graph: nodes are states, edges are the legal moves between them
Board / tile games asking 'minimum dice rolls / jumps to finish'
antiSignals: Edges have different costs → Dijkstra, not plain BFS
You need ALL paths or the longest path → DFS / DP, not BFS
remember.takeaway: Snakes and Ladders is BFS hiding behind a board game. The only real work is the index math to flatten the boustrophedon grid; once squares are numbered 1…n², it's the same shortest-path-on-unweighted-graph BFS as Word Ladder, Open the Lock, and Minimum Genetic Mutation.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise 'minimum number of moves on an unweighted graph' as BFS, can model squares as nodes with up-to-6 edges, and can correctly translate the boustrophedon (snake) numbering into (row, col) coordinates.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using DFS (which finds *a* path, not the shortest), chaining snakes/ladders (a jump should be applied only once), or getting the boustrophedon row/column conversion wrong.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State 'unweighted ⇒ BFS' explicitly, isolate the coordinate conversion into a clean helper, mark visited at enqueue keyed by destination, and note that a snake/ladder is a single forced jump, never chained.

problemStatement:
You are given an `n x n` integer matrix `board` where the cells are labeled from `1` to `n²` in a **Boustrophedon style** starting from the bottom left of the board (i.e. `board[n - 1][0]`) and alternating direction each row.

You start on square `1`. In each move, starting from square `curr`, you may choose a destination square `next` with a label in the range `[curr + 1, min(curr + 6, n²)]` (simulating a 6-sided die). If `board[r][c] != -1`, the square has a snake or ladder and you must move to `board[r][c]` (you do not roll again).

Return *the least number of moves required to reach the square `n²`*. If it is not possible to reach the square, return `-1`.
constraints: grid[i][j] is either -1 or in the range [1, n²]
The squares labeled 1 and n² do not have any ladders or snakes
understanding: Number the squares 1…n² following the snake-like path that starts at the bottom-left and zig-zags up. From any square you can jump 1–6 ahead (a dice roll). Landing on a snake or ladder forces you to its other end. We want the fewest dice rolls to reach the last square — a classic shortest-path-on-an-unweighted-graph question.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How exactly are the squares numbered?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Boustrophedon: square 1 is the bottom-left cell, the bottom row runs left-to-right, the next row up runs right-to-left, and so on. I'll write a helper to convert a label back to (row, col).

clarifyingQuestions.question: If I land on a ladder/snake, do I roll again or chain to another ladder?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Neither — the jump is forced and applied exactly once. You do not roll from the landing square, and a destination that itself holds a snake/ladder is not chained.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Since every move is one dice roll, are all edges equal weight?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — each move costs 1 regardless of where the die or a ladder takes you. Equal weights mean BFS gives the shortest path; Dijkstra would be overkill.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the end square is unreachable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return -1. BFS detects this when the queue empties before n² is ever dequeued.

examples.explanation: From square 1 a roll to 2 takes the ladder to 15. From 15 reach 17, then 13 via the snake, then to 35 via the ladder, finishing at 36 (n²) in 4 moves.
n=2 so n²=4. Square 1 is board[1][0]. A single roll can reach square 4 directly, so the answer is 1.
Snakes/ladders that point back keep you from ever reaching the final square — BFS empties the queue and returns -1.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Equal-cost moves make BFS the only sensible choice for the minimum number of rolls.

approaches.name: BFS Layer-by-Layer (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Phrase it as 'minimum moves on an unweighted graph is textbook BFS — the only twist is the snake-style numbering'.
hints: Each square 1…n² is a node. From square x you can roll to x+1 … x+6, so each node has up to 6 outgoing edges, every edge costing one move.
Equal edge cost ⇒ BFS finds the fewest moves. Process the queue one layer at a time and the layer number is the move count.
The fiddly part is mapping a label back to (row, col): rows are numbered bottom-up, and alternate direction. Write a helper, and remember a snake/ladder is a single forced jump.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n² squares; each is enqueued at most once (visited guard) and explores ≤ 6 neighbours, so the work is O(6·n²) = O(n²). The visited array and queue are O(n²) space.
approaches.explanation:
Strip away the board-game dressing and this is the most standard shortest-path problem there is.

**Why BFS and not DFS or Dijkstra.** A 'move' is one dice roll, and every roll costs exactly the same — one. When all edges have equal weight, BFS explores the graph in concentric layers of increasing distance, so the *first* time it reaches a node it has reached it by a shortest path. DFS would find *a* path but not necessarily the shortest, and Dijkstra's priority queue is wasted machinery on a uniform-cost graph. So the moment you read 'least number of moves' over equal-cost edges, BFS is the answer.

**Modeling the board as a graph.** Each square `x` (1…n²) is a node. The legal moves from `x` are exactly the labels `x+1` through `min(x+6, n²)` — the six faces of the die, clipped at the final square. That's the edge set; there's no adjacency list to build because the edges are implicit in the arithmetic.

**The boustrophedon conversion is the only real work.** Squares are numbered from the bottom-left, snaking upward: the bottom row goes left-to-right, the row above goes right-to-left, and so on. To read `board[r][c]` for a label we invert that numbering. Let `q = (label-1) / n` and `r = (label-1) % n`. The row from the *top* is `n-1-q` (because numbering starts at the bottom). Whether the column runs forward or backward depends on the parity of `q`: even rows-from-bottom go left-to-right (`col = r`), odd ones go right-to-left (`col = n-1-r`). Getting this parity wrong is the single most common bug, so isolate it in a helper and test it on a couple of labels.

**Forced jumps, applied once.** After computing the landing square `next`, peek at its board value. If it's `-1`, you simply stop there. Otherwise a snake or ladder *forces* you to `board[r][c]` — and that's the square you actually occupy. Crucially, you do **not** chain: even if the destination of a ladder itself holds another snake, you take exactly one jump per move. Mark *that final destination* visited and enqueue it, never the intermediate roll square.

**Counting moves by layers.** We process the queue one full layer at a time, incrementing `moves` after each layer drains. Because BFS reaches every node by its shortest distance, the layer index at which `n²` is first dequeued is precisely the minimum number of moves. If the queue empties first, `n²` is unreachable and we return `-1`.
approaches.insight: The hard part of this 'graph' problem isn't the graph algorithm — it's the indexing. Once you trust 'unweighted shortest path ⇒ BFS', the entire challenge collapses to one correct coordinate-conversion helper. Naming that split out loud ('BFS is trivial; let me get the boustrophedon math right') is exactly the structured thinking interviewers reward.

dryRun.intro: Squares: 1=board[1][0], 2=board[1][1], 3=board[0][1], 4=board[0][0]. Start at 1, BFS by layers.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def snakesAndLadders(self, board: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    n = len(board)

    def to_coord(label: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
        quotient, remainder = divmod(label - 1, n)
        row = n - 1 - quotient  # numbering starts at the bottom
        col = remainder if quotient % 2 == 0 else n - 1 - remainder
        return row, col

    visited = [False] * (n * n + 1)
    queue = deque([1])
    visited[1] = True
    moves = 0
    while queue:
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            label = queue.popleft()
            if label == n * n:
                return moves
            for nxt in range(label + 1, min(label + 6, n * n) + 1):
                r, c = to_coord(nxt)
                dest = board[r][c]
                target = nxt if dest == -1 else dest  # forced jump, once
                if not visited[target]:
                    visited[target] = True  # mark on enqueue
                    queue.append(target)
        moves += 1
    return -1

java.explanation: Start the BFS from square 1, marked visited so it's never re-enqueued.
First time the goal is dequeued, the current layer count is the shortest distance.

pitfalls: Using DFS — finds a path, not the shortest one.
Chaining snakes/ladders instead of applying exactly one forced jump per move.
Marking visited by the rolled square instead of the final destination, allowing duplicates.
Off-by-one in the boustrophedon row/column conversion (forgetting numbering starts at the bottom).

approaches.name: BFS with a Distance Array
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as a tidy alternative that stores each square's distance instead of counting layers — handy if the interviewer also wants the distance to every square.
hints: Instead of processing whole layers, store dist[square] = fewest moves to reach it, initialised to -1 (unseen).
When you pop a square, its dist is final; set each unseen neighbour's dist to dist[current] + 1 and enqueue.
dist[n²] is the answer (still -1 if unreachable). The visited check is simply 'dist == -1'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Same graph, same traversal: each square enqueued once, ≤ 6 neighbours each → O(n²) time. The dist array is O(n²) space and doubles as the visited marker.
approaches.explanation:
This is the same BFS with different bookkeeping — instead of an explicit layer loop, each node carries its own distance.

**Distance replaces the layer counter.** We keep an array `dist` where `dist[s]` is the minimum moves to reach square `s`, initialised to `-1` to mean 'not yet seen'. `dist[1] = 0` seeds the start. When we dequeue square `label`, BFS guarantees `dist[label]` is already its shortest distance, so any newly discovered neighbour `target` gets `dist[target] = dist[label] + 1`.

**The dist array is also the visited set.** A square is unvisited exactly when its distance is still `-1`. Checking `dist[target] == -1` before relaxing both prevents re-enqueueing and preserves the shortest distance already recorded — because in unweighted BFS the *first* assignment is always the smallest. This folds two data structures (visited + distance) into one.

**Reading off the answer.** We can return early the moment we set or pop `n²`, but it's just as clean to run BFS to completion and return `dist[n²]` — which is `-1` automatically if the goal was never reached. That uniform handling of the unreachable case is the small ergonomic win of this version.

**Same forced-jump logic.** The coordinate conversion and the single-jump snake/ladder rule are identical to the layer version; only the move-counting mechanism changes. Pick whichever you find less error-prone under pressure — many people prefer the distance array because it removes the inner 'for each node in this layer' loop and its off-by-one risks.
approaches.insight: Layer-counting and a distance array are two interchangeable ways to track BFS depth. The distance array shines when you need the distance to *every* node, not just the goal, and it elegantly returns -1 for unreachable targets with no special-casing.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def snakesAndLadders(self, board: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    n = len(board)

    def to_coord(label: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
        quotient, remainder = divmod(label - 1, n)
        row = n - 1 - quotient
        col = remainder if quotient % 2 == 0 else n - 1 - remainder
        return row, col

    dist = [-1] * (n * n + 1)
    dist[1] = 0
    queue = deque([1])
    while queue:
        label = queue.popleft()
        if label == n * n:
            return dist[label]
        for nxt in range(label + 1, min(label + 6, n * n) + 1):
            r, c = to_coord(nxt)
            dest = board[r][c]
            target = nxt if dest == -1 else dest
            if dist[target] == -1:
                dist[target] = dist[label] + 1
                queue.append(target)
    return dist[n * n]

java.explanation: -1 marks unseen squares; the start square is distance 0.
Goal popped → its recorded distance is the minimum number of moves.
Relax only unseen squares; first assignment is the shortest in unweighted BFS.
If never reached it stays -1, giving the unreachable answer for free.

python.explanation: Single array serves as both visited marker and distance store.
Unseen check; prevents re-enqueueing and overwriting a shorter distance.
One more move than the square we came from.
-1 by default if the goal was unreachable.

edgeCases.behavior: dist[n²] is never set, stays -1, returned at the end.
dist[n²] set to 1 on the first pop → returned as 1.
400 squares, ≤6 edges each — well within O(n²).

pitfalls: Initialising dist to 0 instead of -1 — then the start can't be distinguished from unseen squares.
Updating dist for an already-seen square — corrupts the shortest distance.
Reusing the layer-loop AND the dist array together, double-counting moves.

commonMistakes: Reaching for DFS — it finds a path but not the minimum number of moves.
Chaining consecutive snakes/ladders instead of taking exactly one forced jump per move.
Botching the boustrophedon coordinate conversion (wrong row parity or forgetting numbering starts at the bottom).
Marking visited by the rolled square rather than the final destination after a jump.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Chaining snakes and ladders
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A move is one dice roll plus at most one forced jump. If the landing square has a ladder, you take it once; you do NOT then follow a snake/ladder at that destination. Chaining computes wrong distances.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
r, c = to_coord(nxt)
while board[r][c] != -1:        # wrong: chains jumps
    nxt = board[r][c]
    r, c = to_coord(nxt)
target = nxt
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
r, c = to_coord(nxt)
dest = board[r][c]
target = nxt if dest == -1 else dest   # single forced jump

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong boustrophedon row/column math
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Numbering starts at the bottom-left and alternates direction. Forgetting that rows count up from the bottom, or that odd rows reverse, maps labels to the wrong cell and reads the wrong board value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using DFS for a shortest-path question
commonMistakesDetailed.why: DFS dives down one branch and may reach the goal via a long path first. Only BFS, exploring by increasing distance, guarantees the minimum number of moves on an unweighted graph.
